record.paper_title: Some Open Problems in Topological Algebra
record.original_question: If G is a bounded semitopological group, or more generally a bounded quasitopological group, must G have countable cellularity? Here a semitopological group is a group whose topology is invariant under both left and right shifts, a quasitopological group is a semitopological group with continuous inversion, and bounded means both left bounded and right bounded.

evidence.quote: Problem 6 (Protasov). Let G be a bounded semitopological (quasitopological) group. Has G countable cellularity?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A semitopological group is a group $G$ equipped with a topology such that for every $a\in G$ both the left shift $x\mapsto ax$ and the right shift $x\mapsto xa$ are continuous self-maps of $G$. A quasitopological group is a semitopological group in which inversion $x\mapsto x^{-1}$ is also continuous. A subset $B\subseteq G$ is called left bounded if for every neighborhood $U$ of the identity there exists a finite set $F\subseteq G$ with $B\subseteq FU$, and right bounded if for every such $U$ there is a finite $F\subseteq G$ with $B\subseteq UF$; the group $G$ itself is called bounded if it is both left bounded and right bounded as a subset of itself. The cellularity of a topological space $X$ is the supremum of cardinalities of families of pairwise disjoint nonempty open subsets of $X$, and $X$ has countable cellularity if this supremum is at most $\aleph_0$.

Question: Must every bounded semitopological group have countable cellularity? More generally, must every bounded quasitopological group have countable cellularity?
